title: When the Well Burns
premise: Kestrel Amberdale, a hospice nurse who hears the dying count backwards, returns to their late grandmother's isolated farmhouse to settle the estate. They discover every photograph now contains an extra empty chair, and the dying patients' backwards counting was never a symptom—it was a warning about something that counts down to what it takes. As night falls, Kestrel learns their grandmother spent decades keeping a bargain with a presence beneath the old well: invisibility in exchange for feeding it names. Kestrel must survive until sunrise while unraveling which of their neighbors—and which version of themselves—was invited in, ultimately choosing to give the well their true name rather than let it claim the village's children, ending the bargain at the cost of being forgotten by everyone who ever knew them.
about_author: Silas Dunmore is the pen name of a former rural hospice worker who spent eleven years listening to the last words of the dying in three counties. They write horror from a farmhouse with too many chairs and refuse to explain why.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. At Hollowbrook Hospice, patient Edith Marsh counts backwards from one hundred and dies exactly at zero—the fourth this month. Kestrel notices each counter died on a date matching numbers in an old ledger they've never seen. Emotional beat: professional calm cracking into dread as Kestrel realizes the counting isn't random.

chapters.title: Grandmother's House
chapters.summary: Kestrel arrives at the Amberdale farmhouse for the estate reading, carrying grandma Maren's ashes and her strange instructions: keep the lights on, count the doors nightly. The house feels watched. A neighbor, Hollis Vane, warns them not to stay past dark. Emotional beat: grief tangled with unease; belonging to a place that feels hostile.

chapters.title: One Chair Too Many
chapters.summary: Kestrel sorts through photo albums and finds the impossible: every family photograph, across sixty years, now includes an extra wooden chair no one remembers. In the oldest photos, someone is beginning to sit in it—a blur forming. Emotional beat: vertigo of identity, as Kestrel finds their own childhood face subtly wrong.

chapters.title: What Maren Kept Below
chapters.summary: Kestrel finds Maren's hidden journal behind the pantry wall, learning of the bargain made in 1963: the thing under the well would leave the town unseen if fed a name each generation. Maren's name was next. Emotional beat: betrayal and love colliding—grandmother as protector and jailer.

chapters.title: Hollis Knows
chapters.summary: Hollis Vane's POV. He confesses his family helped broker the original bargain and that his brother was 'taken by the well' in 1989. He begs Kestrel to burn the house and flee before midnight. Emotional beat: guilt-ridden complicity; the price of survival paid by others.

chapters.title: Doors Out of Order
chapters.summary: Back in Kestrel's POV, dusk falls and the door count comes up wrong—eleven doors in a nine-room house. The extra chair sits at the kitchen table, warm. Phone lines die; the road out loops back to the farmhouse. Emotional beat: claustrophobic entrapment, invisibility revoked.

chapters.title: The Names It Ate
chapters.summary: Reading deeper into the journal, Kestrel discovers the taken aren't dead—they're remembered wrongly, wearing borrowed lives. One entry describes 'Kestrel Amberdale' written in Maren's hand decades before Kestrel was born. Emotional beat: identity shatters; Kestrel questions whether they were ever real or always the offering.

chapters.title: Midnight at the Well
chapters.summary: Kestrel descends to the stone well as the chair drags itself behind them like a pallbearer. The presence speaks in the voices of the counted dead, offering a trade: Kestrel's name freely given buys the town another sixty years—or it takes the children instead. Emotional beat: terror transmuting into terrible clarity.

chapters.title: Sunrise Bargain
chapters.summary: Climax. Kestrel speaks their true name into the well—not the one on their birth certificate, but the self they've hidden their whole life—and steps into the chair as dawn breaks. The well accepts; the chair burns to ash; Hollis watches from the treeline, already forgetting why he came. Emotional beat: sacrifice as self-acceptance.

chapters.title: Nobody's Nurse
chapters.summary: Weeks later, a hospice nurse with no records and no past works the night shift at Hollowbrook, hearing no more counting. In the break room, a new photograph on the wall shows staff she doesn't know—including a face that feels like home. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; belonging achieved only through erasure, and perhaps, quietly, peace.
